Compiling and targets

Codegen targets#

Faber has one language and many compilation contracts. Not every feature must lower to every target. This page documents which features each target supports, erases, warns on, or rejects.

Policy verbs#

VerbMeaning
SupportLowers with intended semantics
EraseTypechecks; codegen drops target-specific semantics
WarnLegal Faber; no effect or degraded behaviour on target
RejectCheck or emit fails with explicit diagnostic
DeferParses/binds; lowering not implemented for any target
LimitedStable contract with explicit subset gates

Target table#

One front end and two intermediate representations (a typed HIR and a MIR) feed about two dozen code generators. HIR targets emit readable source in another language; MIR targets lower further, to IR, kernels or native code. Every target is held to the same reference: the MIR runner (faber run). A generated program is correct when its output and exit status match the runner's; a construct a target cannot express yet is rejected by name (unsupported on target <t>: <construct>), never approximated.

How mature each target is, measured on the corpus (662 programs the suite runs, each with expected output; 134 more are meant to be refused). "Suite" counts are cases that pass in corpus-suites/full (faber corpus) out of the cases the suite applies to; the rest are pinned expected failures. C and Haskell have no corpus lane: each single-file program the runner passes was emitted, built with the real toolchain, and its output and exit status compared with the runner's.

Notes:

  • Emit and match counts compare the emitted program's output and exit status with the runner's, for the single-file programs the runner passes; "emit" alone means source was produced, not that it built.
  • The C and Cranelift targets are previews and are on by default in faber. Neither runs under faber run, and a construct either cannot express yet is rejected by name. faber targets on the binary you are running is the authority on what that binary can emit, and a target missing from the build is rejected with PKG001 target_not_in_this_build.
  • The experimental historical targets (Fortran, COBOL, Pascal, Odin, BASIC) cover a deliberate subset (scalars, text, simple collections) and reject the rest by name. They exist partly as a test of the rule that targets implement Faber and never the reverse. They are default-off features and are not in the released faber.
  • Standard-library I/O (files, processes, clocks, network) is wired on the Rust target today; most other targets reject programs that use it, which accounts for much of the gap between their counts and Rust's.
  • "Public" means the generator's source is in the public repository. "Official binary" means it ships in the released faber but its source does not.
  • The GPU rows are kernel functions only. faber run --device metal launches @ kernel functions on a real GPU (Apple silicon); --device cuda is selectable but hardware-gated, and fails closed where no CUDA runtime is registered, as in the default macOS build. -t metal-text, -t wgsl-text and -t llvm-text themselves remain emit-only.
  • The table is generated from the corpus suite at release time, not edited by hand.

Pipeline routing#

Source → Lex → Parse → Collect → Resolve → Lower → Typecheck → Analysis
                                                              ↓
                                    ┌─────────────────────────┴──────────┐
                                    │                                    │
                              HIR backends                        MIR backends
                                    │                                    │
   Rust · Faber · TS · Go · Swift · Python · Haskell · C       fmir · wasm · llvm · metal · wgsl · sexp · basic

Do not read Metal/WGSL percentages on the [target matrix](/toolchain/target-matrix.html) as product completeness. Those rows score full-language corpus terms against a kernel-only emitter. Device runs go through faber run --device metal|cuda (see device execution).

For the device-kernel summary (how a device program runs and what each device target emits) see Target matrix · Device kernel support.

For live capability flags, run faber targets.

Full lowerability matrix#

The large term × target tables (HIR application lane and MIR systems lane) live on the Target compatibility page. That matrix is generated from grammar/EBNF_MATRIX.md and reports term lowerability only — not erase/warn policy, and not GPU product health. GPU backends and the “why no CUDA column?” note are explained in that page’s summary.

Compilation lanes#

Faber has a single shared frontend — lex, parse, typecheck — and then forks into multiple lowering routes depending on what the target needs. The intermediate representations form a pipeline: source is analysed into HIR, optionally lowered to MIR, and optionally detoured through AIR before final emission. Each IR serves a distinct purpose, and each target consumes from whichever IR matches its needs.

Pipeline overview#

Source (.fab)  →  Lex  →  Parse  →  Collect  →  Resolve  →  Lower  →  Typecheck  →  Analysis
                                                              │
                                                    HIR (semantic core)
                                                    ┌─────┴─────┐
                                                    │           │
                                              Reader locale    MIR lowering
                                              (input/output)    │
                                                                │
                                                      ┌─────────┴─────────┐
                                                      │                   │
                                                CPU lanes           GPU lanes
                                                      │                   │
                                            ┌────┬────┼────┬────┐     ┌───┴───────┐
                                            │    │    │    │    │     │           │
                                          FMIR LLVM WASM  TS  Go   WGSL   Metal

The same frontend serves every target. After semantic analysis produces the HIR, the compiler chooses a route based on the target:

  • HIR-direct — emit directly from typed HIR for language-shaped backends (Rust, Faber, TypeScript, Go, Swift, Python, Haskell, C)
  • HIR → MIR — lower to execution-shaped MIR, then emit for systems and low-level targets
  • HIR → MIR → AIR → MIR — detour through pure-functional AIR for autodiff and fusion transforms, then rejoin MIR

HIR — High-Level Intermediate Representation#

The HIR is the truth. It is a typed, language-shaped IR that preserves declarations, type information, and structural relationships. Every Faber program, regardless of its original locale or target destination, passes through this representation.

Reader locale integration#

Reader locale operates through the HIR. A Faber source file written in Thai keywords is parsed and lowered into the same HIR as the equivalent Latin source. The locale is a surface rendering of the HIR, not a fork in the semantic core.

  • Input: localised source (Thai, Chinese, Arabic, etc.) → normalised HIR — shipped
  • Output: HIR → localised source re-emission — shipped (faber convert --to <locale>)

faber convert --to th-TH round-trips any Faber source through the HIR and emits it with Thai keywords, completing the symmetry: the same HIR can produce any locale surface, just as it can produce any target backend. faber format re-emits through the same HIR at the file's own locale and does not translate.

HIR-direct backends#

These targets emit directly from the typed HIR without lowering to MIR. They preserve source-level structure longer and are suited for language-shaped output:

TargetStatusRole
RustSupportWidest package product surface today (a Cargo project; the best-covered standard-library I/O). One projection of HIR — not the semantic center.
FaberSupportCanonical source view through the HIR-backed re-emitter (faber format / faber convert). Round-trip stability.
TypeScriptProbeHIR-direct file emission; see the target table for measured counts. Not a package product path yet.
GoEraseHIR-direct file emission; see the target table for measured counts; borrow modes erased.
Swift, Python, HaskellProbeHIR-direct file emission; see the target table for measured counts.
CPreviewHIR-direct C11 with a header-only runtime; its source is in the public repository.

MIR — Mid-Level Intermediate Representation#

MIR is the execution-shaped IR. It represents control flow, locals, runtime calls, places, branches, and error edges — the facts that low-level targets need. Where HIR preserves source structure, MIR flattens it into a control-flow graph.

HIR → MIR lowering translates language-shaped constructs into execution steps. MIR is validated after lowering to catch structural issues before any backend attempts emission.

Semantic ownership. Faber maintains a clear boundary between rules enforced in the HIR/MIR (type checking, definite assignment, borrow mode lints) and rules left to target toolchains (Rust lifetime analysis, Go type safety). This prevents the compiler from duplicating work that target compilers already do correctly.

AIR detour#

AIR (Autograd / AI Representation) is a pure-functional transform detour off the HIR → MIR path. It is entered by explicit annotation on individual functions:

@ radix lane "air"
fn identity(bool value) → bool {
    return value
}

main {
    print identity(true)
}

The annotation needs a package whose [build] target is a MIR target (here target = "fmir"); on a bare file the default Rust target reports TARGETLANE001 lane_requires_mir_backed_target.

AIR-lane functions must satisfy a purity policy — no mutation, no effects, no loops. Functions that violate this are rejected with a diagnostic before AIR lowering begins. The rest of the program continues to use ordinary Faber with mutation, effects, and loops.

After the AIR transforms complete their work (autodiff and fusion — both shipped), the result is re-lowered to MIR and rejoins the ordinary MIR backend pipeline. AIR owns no backends and no independent typechecker — it is a transform checkpoint, not a parallel IR.

HIR  →  AIR purity check  →  HIR to AIR lowering  →  AIR validation  →  AIR to MIR re-lowering  →  MIR backend

This architecture mirrors JAX's approach: keep a pure-functional representation for transforms, lower to imperative IR only at the end. AIR exists because running autodiff over imperative MIR would require reconstructing purity from code that was lowered into mutation.

CPU target lanes#

CPU targets consume MIR and produce either executable artifacts or text for external toolchains. Faber emits text where possible and relies on lower-level toolchains for the final compilation step — analogous to how a C compiler emits assembly for the assembler and linker.

FMIR — Faber's own MIR runtime#

FMIR is the MIR-native package executor. The compiler extracts MIR into a binary payload and wraps it with a short Rust kernel loader. This produces a self-contained executable that runs the MIR through Faber's in-process runner — no separate runtime installation required.

FormatDescription
fmir-textInspectable FMIR text image at target/faber-mir/image.fmir.txt
fmirCompact binary FMIR image at target/faber-mir/image.fmir
fmir-binSelf-contained runner at target/faber-mir/exe/run — embeds FMIR bytes

LLVM text#

Faber emits LLVM IR as text (.ll), not as integrated LLVM codegen. The emitted IR is intended for external toolchain steps — verification, optimisation, and native code generation are handled by downstream LLVM tools. This is a staging and validation target, not a native codegen path embedded in the compiler.

WASM#

Faber emits WebAssembly text (.wat). -t wasm-text is the name; -t wasm is an alias kept for compatibility, and converting the text to a binary module is an external-tool step (wat2wasm or wasm-tools). The emitted module uses external host imports (faber_* runtime symbols). Wasm is a supported-with-limitations target: it proves the MIR lowering pipeline for an open standard format, but there is no host runtime yet and it is not a package delivery runtime.

TypeScript, Go, Swift, Python and Haskell (HIR-direct)#

These are HIR-direct file-emission targets: they validate that Faber's semantics translate into widely used type systems. Measured counts are in the target table above. Full package build and run workflows center on the Rust package path today, and standard-library I/O is wired on the Rust target — that is a packaging convenience, not a claim that HIR meaning lives in Rust.

C (preview)#

The C target emits one C11 translation unit from the typed HIR, with a header-only runtime (runtime/c/faber.h). It lives in the public repository and is a preview: it covers a growing subset (exact integer arithmetic, control flow, functions, text, lists, classes and floats) and rejects everything else by name (unsupported on target c: <construct>). The emitted program never reaches undefined behavior; the corpus checks it under the undefined-behavior and address sanitizers. It is on by default in faber, and a GCC or Clang compiler builds the output.

fn fib(int n) → int {
    if n ≺ 2 then return n
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
}

main {
    mut int total ← 0
    mut int i ← 0
    while i ≺ 10 {
        total ← total + fib(i)
        i ← i + 1
    }
    print "sum of the first ten Fibonacci numbers: §"(total)
    print -7 / 2
}

faber emit -t c fib.fab writes this (the runner prints 88 and -4; the built program prints the same):

/* Generated by radix; do not edit. Needs the Faber C runtime header:
   compile with -I <runtime>/c (runtime/c in the Faber tree). */
#include "faber.h"

static int64_t f_fib(faber_arena *, int64_t);

static int64_t f_fib(faber_arena *faber_a, int64_t p_n) {
    if (p_n < INT64_C(2)) {
        return p_n;
    }
    return faber_store_i64((__extension__ ({ int64_t faber_t0 = f_fib(faber_a, (__extension__ ({ int faber_o = 0; int64_t faber_r = faber_sub_o(p_n, INT64_C(1), &faber_o); faber_o ? faber_store_i64(faber_sub(p_n, INT64_C(1)), "argument") : faber_r; }))); int64_t faber_t1 = f_fib(faber_a, (__extension__ ({ int faber_o = 0; int64_t faber_r = faber_sub_o(p_n, INT64_C(2), &faber_o); faber_o ? faber_store_i64(faber_sub(p_n, INT64_C(2)), "argument") : faber_r; }))); faber_add(faber_t0, faber_t1); })), "return");
}

int main(void) {
    faber_arena faber_root = {0};
    faber_arena *const faber_a = &faber_root;
    int64_t l_total = INT64_C(0);
    int64_t l_i = INT64_C(0);
    while (l_i < INT64_C(10)) {
        l_total = faber_store_i64((__extension__ ({ int64_t faber_t2 = l_total; int64_t faber_t3 = f_fib(faber_a, l_i); faber_add(faber_t2, faber_t3); })), "assignment to `total`");
        l_i = (__extension__ ({ int faber_o = 0; int64_t faber_r = faber_add_o(l_i, INT64_C(1), &faber_o); faber_o ? faber_store_i64(faber_add(l_i, INT64_C(1)), "assignment to `i`") : faber_r; }));
    }
    printf("%s\n", faber_join(faber_a, 2, "sum of the first ten Fibonacci numbers: ", faber_int_text(faber_a, l_total)));
    printf("%" PRId64 "\n", -INT64_C(4));
    return 0;
}

Build it with cc -std=c11 -I <runtime>/c fib.c -o fib -lm.

GPU target lanes#

WGSL (via WGPU)#

Faber emits WGSL compute shader source through the MIR pipeline. The emitted WGSL is validated through naga (30.x) and includes a reflection sidecar for bind-group metadata. This covers the device-safe kernel subset: rank-1 f32 device views are supported; rank-2 views reject. WGSL is not a GPU launch runtime — Faber emits the shader source, but execution requires an external WebGPU runtime. The Triga library supplies the typed geometry, scene, and resource contracts consumed by a WebGPU host.

Metal#

Metal compute shader text emission follows the same pattern as WGSL: Faber emits Metal Shading Language source for the device-safe kernel subset. Metal and CUDA are the device execution paths (faber run --device metal|cuda). Metal is the Apple Silicon local-dev and API-parity host; CUDA is the NVIDIA deployment host. WebGPU remains a browser graphics and headless lane (Triga), not a package device-execution path.

Device execution (Metal / CUDA)#

A package carries a device program when its source declares an @ kernel compute kernel and its manifest declares a [device] section. `faber run --device reference|cpu|metal|cuda|auto` runs it through the host driver and fails closed with stable codes (E_BACKEND_UNAVAILABLE, E_DEVICE_*, E_NO_DEVICE_PROGRAM) instead of silently falling back to the CPU. reference runs kernels as ordinary functions on the MIR runner and is the oracle device results are checked against.

Architecture note#

Faber's compilation architecture is similar in spirit to how the Rust compiler works. Rust lowers through HIR → MIR → LLVM IR, embedding the LLVM toolchain directly for final native codegen. Faber takes a softer approach: it emits text for external toolchains (LLVM text, WGSL, Metal, WAT) rather than embedding them, while reserving direct code emission for its own runtime (FMIR) and its widest package product surface today (Rust, where Cargo and rustc handle the downstream pipeline).

The text-emission approach means Faber never needs to bundle LLVM, a Wasm runtime, or a GPU driver — those remain external dependencies chosen by the user. The tradeoff is that Faber cannot offer a single-command build for every target; the user must install the appropriate toolchain for their chosen backend.

Target summary#

The target table above is the summary: what each target emits and how well it matches the runner. build, run, and package describe Faber workflows; external toolchains (rustc, wasm-tools, naga, clang) handle final compilation for text-emission targets.

Full measured grammar × target lowerability (every corpus term, HIR and MIR columns): Target compatibility.

Compiler performance#

Radix's front end runs in-process and single-threaded, and faber check and faber run never invoke an external toolchain. For faber build -t rust the user-perceived time is dominated by Cargo and rustc, not by Faber's front end. Reuse one Cargo target directory across builds so the compiled runtime crate stays cached; building each program into a fresh target/ pays the runtime crate's compile cost every time.
